title: Diversity
text:
Introduction
LoggingDiversity is a sub-project of the BioForest project aimed at studying the Interactions between tree biodiversity, forest dynamics and climate in managed tropical forests with a pan-tropical approach. Specifically, LoggingDiversity focus on the effects of logging disturbance on tropical forest diversity - a global assessment with the following question: What is the effect of logging intensity on biodiversity, and how does it change through time?

title: Data
text:
Rarefied species richness
For each site and plot, we further investigated the raredfied species richness using a jackknife procedure to build the rarefaction curve and expressing species richness equivalent to 100 trees. The metric corrects for the variation of number of stems in time, but not number of tree identified to the species level, and botanist expertise. However, as trajectories will be relatively modelled per plot, we may assume that they are comparable.

title: Model
text:
Old
We modelled the recovery of species richness over time using a model derived from the common framework for modelling the recovery of disturbed tropical forests (Maurent et al. 2023).
The recovery trajectory of species \(richness\) over \(time\) after disturbance is modelled using a long-term process LTP of recovery and a short-term process STP that allows for intermediate extremes (minimums or maximums) of species \(richness\) at intermediate times. This results in the following equation:
\[\begin{align}
log(richness) \sim \mathcal N (log(\mu), \sigma)\\
\mu = \theta_{plot} \times (\phi_{plot} + LTP \times (1 - \phi_{plot}) + STP) \\
\end{align}\]
With \(\theta_{plot}\) the plot asymptotic value of species richness recovery; \(\phi_{plot}\) the plot remaining value of forest attribute relative to the plot asymptotic value just after disturbance (e.g. \(1 - \phi_{plot}\) corresponds to disturbance relative intensity); \(u\) the mean expected species richness in time after disturbance, and \(\sigma\) the unexplained residual variation.
The long-term process \(LTP\) recovery over \(time\) after disturbance is modelled using an exponential recovery with a constant plot relative recovery rate \(\lambda_{plot}\) as follow:
\[\begin{align}
LTP = 1 - e^{-\lambda_{plot} \times time} \\
\end{align}\]
The short-term process \(STP\) that allows for intermediate extremes (minimums or maximums) of species richness at intermediate times is modelled using extremes timing parameters at the site level \(\tau_{site}\) and intensity parameters at the plot level \(\delta_{plot}\), as follows:
\[\begin{align}
STP = \delta_{plot} \times (\frac{time}{\tau_{site}} \times e^{1-\frac{time}{\tau_{site}}})^2 \\
\end{align}\]
We furthered linked the trajectories of species \(richness\) to \(disturbance\) with a hierarchical nested model that describes the relationship between the disturbance intensity of basal area and the intermediate diversity extremes that occur after disturbance, in line with the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, using a linear regression:
\[\begin{align}
\delta_{plot} \sim \mathcal N ( \delta_0+\gamma\times disturbance, \sigma_{\delta})
\end{align}\]
Here, \(\gamma\) represents the linear effect of disturbance intensity on intermediate species richness extremes, and \(\delta_0\) represents its intercept. Thus, a positive \(\gamma\) value directly represents the intermediate disturbance hypothesis expectation.
To update: We used hyperlaw distributions for parameters of plot relative recovery rate plot, extremes timing parameters at the site level site and intensity parameters at the plot level plot with means values , , and and variances , , and . We used normal laws for plot and  site and a cauchy law for plot for forest diversity metrics without assuming it sign and a lognormal law for forest structure assuming only positive values. The full model with associated priors is further described in SI note.
Code
ltp <- function(time, dist, thetainf, lambda) {
  theta0 <- thetainf * dist
  ltp <- 1 - exp(-lambda * time)
  theta0 + (thetainf - theta0) * (ltp)
}
stp <- function(time, dist, thetainf, lambda, tau, delta) {
  theta0 <- thetainf * dist
  ltp <- 1 - exp(-lambda * time)
  stp <- delta * (time / tau * exp(1 - time / tau))^2
  theta0 + ltp * (thetainf - theta0) + stp * thetainf
}
data.frame(time = seq(0.1, 30, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(y_stp_max = stp(time,
    dist = 0.5, thetainf = 20, lambda = 0.05,
    tau = 5, delta = 0.5
  )) |>
  mutate(y_stp_min = stp(time,
    dist = 0.5, thetainf = 20, lambda = 0.05,
    tau = 5, delta = 0.25
  )) |>
  mutate(y_ltp = ltp(time, dist = 0.5, thetainf = 20, lambda = 0.05)) |>
  bind_rows(data.frame(
    time = 0,
    y_stp_max = 20, y_stp_min = 20,
    y_ltp = 20,
    y_ba_max = 30, y_ba_min = 30
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_ltp), col = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_stp_max), col = "#a7d6ac") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_stp_min), col = "#a7d6ac", alpha = .5) +

  ) +

library(cmdstanr)
out <- file.path("chains", "raw")
if (file.exists(out)) {
  unlink(out, recursive = TRUE)
}
dir.create(out)
model <- cmdstan_model("models/model.stan")
data <- read_tsv("data/derived_data/data.tsv")
ind <- data |>
  select(site, sitenum, plot, plotnum, dist_obs) %>%
  unique()
data_u <- ind |>
  left_join(filter(data, rel_year <= 0))
data_r <- ind |>
  left_join(filter(data, rel_year > 0))
mdata <- list(
  n = nrow(data_r),
  s = max(data_r$sitenum),
  p = max(data_r$plotnum),
  y = data_r$diversity_q0_sp,
  t = data_r$rel_year,
  site = data_r$sitenum,
  plot = data_r$plotnum,
  site_plot = ind$sitenum,
  n_u = nrow(data_u),
  y_u = data_u$diversity_q0_sp,
  plot_u = data_u$plotnum,
  dist_p = ind$dist_obs
)
fit <- model$sample(
  mdata,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 4,
  save_warmup = FALSE,
  refresh = 100,
  output_dir = out
)

title: Sensitivity
text:
Data
We explored the role of plot area in model sensitivity, particularly with regard to the site parameters representing the linear effect of forest structure disturbance on intermediate diversity extremes. For this, we focused on the Paracou and Mbaiki sites, whose original plots are 6.25 and 4 ha respectively, and virtually subdivided them into adjacent plots of 4, 2, 1, 0.5 and 0.25 ha (for reference, the main analyses were conducted using 1-ha virtual plots). To update: We then ran the joint model with basal area and genus diversity using Hill’s number of order 1 for each size, and assessed the sign, significance, strength, and uncertainty of the site parameters.

title: Sensitivity
Sensitivity
text:
Fits


Code
areas <- c(6.25, 4.00, 2.00, 1.00, 0.50, 0.25)
recovery <- cmdstan_model("models/model.stan")
for (a in areas) {
  data_equ <- read_tsv("data/derived_data/sensitivity_data_rec.tsv") |>
    filter(area == a)
  data_rec <- read_tsv("data/derived_data/sensitivity_data_rec.tsv") |>
    filter(area == a)
  ind <- data_rec |>
    select(area, site, plot, subplot, sitenum, subplotnum, dist_obs) |>
    unique()
  mdata <- list(
    n = nrow(data_rec),
    s = max(data_rec$sitenum),
    p = max(data_rec$subplotnum),
    y = data_rec$diversity,
    t = data_rec$rel_year,
    site = data_rec$sitenum,
    plot = data_rec$subplotnum,
    site_plot = ind$sitenum,
    n_u = nrow(data_equ),
    y_u = data_equ$diversity,
    plot_u = data_equ$subplotnum,
    dist_p = ind$dist_obs
  )
  dir <- file.path("chains", paste0("rec", "_", a * 100))
  unlink(dir, recursive = TRUE)
  dir.create(dir)
  fit <- recovery$sample(
    mdata,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    save_warmup = FALSE,
    refresh = 100,
    output_dir = dir
  )
}

title: Meetings
text:
26/09/11 - SUAS?
This appendix can be used to take notes from meetings.
Camille & Sylvain
Following discussions about SUAS’s addition to the dataset, we decided to remove the delta linear regression that linked the plots together in a hyperlaw. Instead, we will perform post hoc linear regression, first quickly and then with uncertainty transmission. Doing so, we hope that SUAS won’t interfere with other super sites, such as Paracou. The analysis of the level of indetermination should be maintained for discussion purposes. The message seems to indicate a positive relationship when not accounting for rarefaction, suggesting an artefact from the increasing number of stems, but there is still a slight positive effect when accounting for it (to check if still the case). The results and discussion will be enriched by the spatial sensitivity analysis of Paracou and Mbaiki, which should be updated with post hoc linear regression with uncertainty transmission for consistency.
